findings.source_passage: No one, except Karl Marx, foresaw radical change. What announced it? The world was producing sixty or seventy million tons of coal
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Even the violent reaction after 1848'
findings.why_it_matters: The 'except Karl Marx' parenthetical is one of the most critically noted moments in the chapter — Adams's wry, retrospective acknowledgment of Marx is a famous ironic aside that shapes interpretations of his historical self-awareness. The draft drops it entirely, writing only 'No one foresaw radical change,' erasing the signature.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'except Karl Marx' verbatim within the sentence: 'No one, except Karl Marx, foresaw radical change.'

findings.source_passage: that the most powerful emotion of man, next to the sexual, should disappear, might be a personal defect of his own; but that the most intelligent society, led by the most intelligent clergy, in the most moral conditions he ever knew, should have solved all the problems of the universe so thoroughly as to have quite ceased making itself anxious about past or future
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Of all the conditions of his youth which afterwards puzzled'
findings.why_it_matters: This is the interpretive climax of Adams's critique of Boston Unitarianism — the 'most powerful emotion of man, next to the sexual' formulation is famously noted by critics as Adams's most daring diagnostic claim, and the extended ironic sentence about 'solving all problems of the universe' is the rhetorical peak of the chapter. The draft skips the entire passage, jumping directly to Parker and Emerson.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore this sentence substantially verbatim; it is both culturally famous and interpretively essential to the chapter's argument about the disappearance of religion.

findings.source_passage: men whose lives were to fall in the generation between 1865 and 1900 had, first of all, to get rid of it, and take the stamp that belonged to their time. This was their education. To outsiders, immigrants, adventurers, it was easy, but the old Puritan nature rebelled against change.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'For any American boy the fact that his father was running'
findings.why_it_matters: The 'This was their education' sentence is a rhetorical pivot that echoes the book's title ironically, and the argument about the 1865–1900 generation is the structural logic behind the chapter's educational thesis. The draft compresses the entire passage to a vague reference to Puritan thought and moral standards, losing the generational framing.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentences about men between 1865 and 1900 having to 'get rid of' the stamp, with the 'This was their education' pivot sentence included.

findings.source_passage: He had nothing but himself to think about. His superiority was, indeed, real and incontestable; he was the classical ornament of the anti-slavery party; their pride in him was unbounded
findings.source_locator: paragraph on Sumner, after 'his solitude was glacial'
findings.why_it_matters: 'He had nothing but himself to think about' is a signature epigram — a devastating, economical portrait that critics single out as Adams's sharpest characterization of Sumner's psychic condition. The draft has 'his solitude was glacial, and reacted on his character' but drops the epigram entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert 'He had nothing but himself to think about' as a standalone sentence after the reference to his glacial solitude.

findings.source_passage: The passionate hatred of school methods was almost a method in itself. Yet the day-school of that time was respectable, and the boy had nothing to complain of. In fact, he never complained. He hated it because he was here with a crowd of other boys and compelled to learn by memory a quantity of things that did not amuse him.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'In any and all its forms, the boy detested school'
findings.why_it_matters: The paradox 'The passionate hatred of school methods was almost a method in itself' is a voice-defining ironic formulation, and the deadpan 'In fact, he never complained' followed immediately by 'He hated it' is signature Adams irony. The draft reduces this entire passage to two flat sentences.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the ironic pivot sentences, particularly 'The passionate hatred of school methods was almost a method in itself' and the deadpan sequence 'he had nothing to complain of. In fact, he never complained.'

findings.source_passage: Never a tone of arrogance! Never a gesture of pride!
findings.source_locator: paragraph on Charles Francis Adams's character, near end
findings.why_it_matters: The draft places these sentences inside quotation marks ('"Never a tone of arrogance! Never a gesture of pride!"'), which misrepresents them as a quotation rather than the narrator's own rhetorical exclamation — a minor but real distortion of the passage's register.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the quotation marks so the exclamatory sentences read as the narrator's voice, not a cited quotation.

summary: Two high-severity losses — the famous 'except Karl Marx' parenthetical erased entirely, and the climactic 'most powerful emotion of man, next to the sexual' religion passage absent — plus three medium-severity voice and interpretive flattenings require regeneration.
